ACLC: Large US companies across industries, actively picked by American Century's managers, with the giant technology and internet companies prominent at the top. It is a core-style stock holding whose results depend on the managers' research rather than index weights, so it will not move exactly with the market.
ACMG: Midsize US growth companies, chosen with American Century's insights models that look for firms whose earnings growth is strengthening. Midsize growers can become tomorrow's large companies, so the fund aims for that runway, accepting bigger swings than a large-company fund along the way.
ACVU: US companies picked for value with a systematic twist: Hartford's process hunts for stocks whose prices lag the strength of their businesses. It is a core-style holding tilted toward cheaper companies, so it tends to trail when expensive growth stocks are leading the market.
AGGB: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds issued in the US. It is the classic core bond holding, meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
AIBN: Corporate bonds issued by the companies building AI infrastructure, such as data center operators and the power and technology firms behind them. It is a way to lend to the AI buildout instead of owning its stocks, trading stock market upside for steadier interest payments.
AIQU: A leveraged bet on artificial intelligence stocks: an exchange-traded note designed to deliver three times the daily move of an AI index. The leverage resets daily, so it is built for short-term trades, and in choppy markets the daily reset can grind its value down even when the index ends flat.
ANG: Fallen angels: corporate bonds that were once rated investment grade and have since been downgraded to high yield, from US and Canadian issuers. The idea is that downgraded companies often work hard to win their good ratings back, so the fund buys their debt at the cheaper, riskier price.
AVUC: US companies of every size, tilted toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms, which Avantis expects to deliver higher returns over time. It works as a core stock holding with a deliberate slant away from the biggest growth names, so it will not hug the index.
BCOM: A broad basket of commodities, energy, metals and farm goods, held through futures contracts that together mirror the overall commodity market. It is a one-fund way to own raw materials, which tend to move differently from stocks and can shine when inflation surprises, though futures add their own quirks.
BSMA: Municipal bonds that all mature around 2036, when the fund itself winds up and returns investors' money, much like holding one bond to maturity. The income is generally free of federal tax, and holding to the end date softens the effect of interest rate swings along the way.
DBAR: Two strategies in one fund: a managed futures program that follows price trends across markets, and a US equity strategy. The blend aims for returns that do not depend on stocks rising, so it is meant to zig when a normal portfolio zags, though it can lag in calm, rising markets.
DDX: A blended portfolio of Treasury bonds and US stocks, managed to keep the whole fund's overall sensitivity to interest rates at a set target, the 10 in its name. Stocks supply the growth and long bonds the rate exposure, so it behaves like neither a pure stock nor a pure bond fund.
DOJE: Direct exposure to Dogecoin, the meme-born cryptocurrency featuring a Shiba Inu dog, held rather than reached through futures. Dogecoin has no fixed supply cap and its price runs almost entirely on sentiment and social media attention, so it is among the swingiest assets in any fund lineup.
EUHY: High yield corporate bonds issued in euros by riskier European and international companies, with a currency hedge that removes most euro swings against the dollar. It pays more interest than safer bond funds, and the hedge means returns hinge on the borrowers' credit rather than on exchange rates.
FTN: Investment-grade corporate bonds in the middle range: loans to solid companies with between five and ten years left until they come due. It sits between short and long bond funds in both interest paid and price swings, a middle-of-the-road core holding for the bond side of a portfolio.
FTPA: Pennsylvania municipal bonds: tax-exempt debt issued by the state, its cities, school districts and authorities to fund public projects. The income is generally free of federal and Pennsylvania tax for state residents, which is the whole point, so it suits Pennsylvanians in higher tax brackets more than anyone else.
GANZ: A thematic fund that rotates into whatever themes the manager favors, holding US-listed stocks alongside options on individual companies and indexes. Nothing about its focus is fixed, so it is a bet on the manager's theme-picking and timing rather than on any one industry or style.
GOLY: Gold exposure paired with investment-grade corporate bonds, a mix designed so the bond side pays interest while the gold side chases the metal's price. The yield enhancement means it will not move exactly with gold, and it gives up some of gold's safe-haven purity for income.
GTOS: Short-term bonds from a mix of issuers, government debt alongside corporate bonds, chosen for total return rather than for safety alone. Keeping durations short means the price moves less when interest rates change, but reaching into corporate credit adds risk a Treasury-only fund would not have.
HH: High yield corporate bonds: dollar-denominated debt from companies with weaker credit, paying extra interest to compensate for the risk. It is an income fund whose fortunes follow the health of riskier borrowers, so it tends to fall when recession fears rise and defaults are in the news.
HINC: High yield corporate bonds chosen by Hartford's managers: below-investment-grade debt from companies that pay extra interest because their finances are weaker. It is an income fund that accepts credit risk for yield, so it falls when investors worry about the economy and defaults.
HSBH: Shares of one company, HSBC, the British banking giant with a big Asian business, held through its US-listed depositary receipts. Like others in this series, it is built to soften the effect of currency moves between the pound and the dollar, leaving the bank's own fortunes as the main driver.
IGB: Investment-grade corporate bonds issued in the US market: loans to solid companies and other strong borrowers, paying interest until maturity. It is a core bond holding, steadier than stock funds but still sensitive to interest rates, and it pays a little more than government bonds of similar length.
JUDB: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks that uses options to absorb a deeper first slice of losses than standard buffers, over an outcome period that resets each July. The trade for that stronger cushion is a tighter cap on gains, and the protection only lines up if shares are held for the full period.
LIGB: Long-dated investment-grade corporate bonds: loans to solid companies with at least ten years until they come due. Long maturities pay a bit more interest than shorter bonds, but the price swings much more when interest rates move, so it is a bolder core bond holding.
MAGC: China's answer to the Magnificent Seven: the seven giant Chinese technology companies, spanning e-commerce, gaming, electric vehicles and internet platforms. It is a highly concentrated bet on China's tech champions, so it swings with Chinese consumer spending, Beijing's regulation and the mood toward Chinese stocks abroad.
MBCE: Blue chip companies, the large established names picked by Monarch's index, which at the moment reaches well beyond old-economy giants into chipmakers and online retail. It is a core-style large company holding, though its current tilt toward technology makes it livelier than a traditional blue chip fund.
MMF: Money market securities: very short-term, high-quality IOUs from governments and strong companies that mature in weeks or months. It is the closest thing to cash in fund form, built to hold value steady and pay a little interest, so its return trails anything that takes real risk.
NUIF: US infrastructure companies: power utilities at about half the fund, energy pipelines and industrial operators making up most of the rest. It is built for steady, fee-and-bill-based income from essential systems, so it tends to move less than the broad market but still feels interest rate changes.
PBSC: Debt that is secured by collateral: bundles of loans and other asset-backed borrowings, actively managed so the mix can flex across secured credit markets. It is an income fund built on loans with assets behind them, which cushions losses compared with unsecured debt but still carries credit risk.
PEPT: Companies advancing peptide-based products: medicines, supplements and cosmetics built from short chains of amino acids, plus the technology that makes them. It is a narrow bet on one corner of biotechnology, the field behind many new weight-loss and metabolic drugs, so it swings with drug trial news.
PSOX: Two unglamorous but essential parts of electronics: multilayer ceramic capacitors, the tiny components on every circuit board, and power semiconductors that manage electricity. It is a supply-chain bet on the components AI data centers and electric vehicles cannot do without, far from the famous chip names.
QQDH: Exposure to the Nasdaq 100's big innovators, wrapped in two options overlays: one sells put spreads for income, the other buys cheap daily crash protection. The design tries to pay income and blunt sudden drops, at the cost of some upside and a more complicated risk profile.
RBTX: Robotics companies and the technology around them: makers of robots, automation systems and the sensors and software that guide them, actively picked worldwide. It is a focused bet on machines taking over more physical work, so it swings with industrial spending and tech sentiment.
SCOP: Actual copper metal held in storage, so the units move with the price of copper rather than with mining companies. Copper is the wiring metal of electrification, used in grids, motors and data centers, so its price swings with industrial demand and construction.
SHEH: Shares of one company, Shell, the global energy giant, held through its US-listed depositary receipts rather than bought on the London exchange. Like others in this series, it is built to soften the effect of currency moves between the pound and the dollar, leaving the stock itself as the main driver.
SLVI: Income built on silver: the fund holds silver funds that own the metal and sells options on them to generate payouts. Silver swings far more than gold, and the options cap part of the upside, so the distributions come with a bumpier ride than most income funds.
SMNG: The Samsung group in one fund: companies of the South Korean conglomerate spanning memory chips and phones, batteries, construction, insurance and biotechnology. It is a single-conglomerate bet, so it concentrates in one country's corporate giant and swings with both the chip cycle and the Korean market.
SMRZ: Companies developing small modular reactors, the next-generation nuclear plants designed to be built in factories and shipped to sites, plus their suppliers. It is a speculative bet on a technology still proving itself commercially, so it can swing hard on policy news and project milestones.
SMTJ: Japanese companies across the economy, led by industrial firms at about a quarter, banks and technology names, picked for those set to gain from long-term changes in Japanese society and industry. It is a single-country fund, so it swings with Japan's market and with the yen.
SSK: Solana, the fast blockchain network's token, held directly, with a staking feature that locks up part of the holding to help run the network and earn extra tokens. Staking adds a trickle of extra return on top of the price, but Solana itself remains highly volatile.
UPSD: Large US companies plus options positioned to add extra upside when the market rises, rather than to protect against falls. It is a growth-leaning core holding with a kicker: the options can amplify good stretches, and they can also expire worthless in flat markets.
VGTX: Technology companies plus options written on them, a combination built to turn the tech sector's movement into income as well as growth. The options trade some upside for payouts, so it behaves like a tech fund with the sharpest rallies trimmed, and tech's usual swings still apply.
VOXP: Large US companies across every major industry, currently led by the giant technology and internet names that dominate the market. It works as a core-style stock holding, and because its top names are the market's biggest, it will move much like the broad US market itself.
WBEM: Companies in emerging markets, the faster-growing economies of Asia, Latin America and beyond, actively picked by William Blair's managers. Emerging stocks can grow quickly but swing hard on politics, currencies and commodity prices, so this is the adventurous end of a foreign stock allocation.
WBIE: Companies outside the US, actively picked by William Blair's managers for growth, across developed and other international markets. It gives a stock portfolio its foreign piece, chosen stock by stock, so currency moves and foreign market moods both shape its returns.
WSML: Small companies from developed markets around the world, thousands of them across every industry, in a single fund. Small stocks swing more than large ones and can outperform for long stretches, so this fills the small-company corner of a global portfolio that big-company funds miss.
WTAL: A long-short fund that bets on some global stocks rising and others falling, using swaps and other derivatives to run both sides at once. It aims to make money from the gap between winners and losers rather than from markets rising, so its results can look nothing like a stock fund's.
XRPR: Direct exposure to XRP, the token of a blockchain network built for fast cross-border payments, held rather than traded through futures. XRP's price is driven by crypto sentiment and by the legal and adoption news around its network, so it swings hard in both directions.
ZVOL: A fund that harvests the volatility premium, mainly by selling VIX futures, which measure expected stock market swings, when they price in more fear than usually arrives. It can earn steadily in calm markets and lose quickly in a crash, so it is a specialist trading tool.
